description: Every example, for finding the ones relevant to a task: examples/tools/find.py searches it, and examples/tags.json defines the tags.

examples.title: A switch cleanup that keeps the money for declined orders
examples.summary: Merging one case into its neighbours makes the code shorter, and it still compiles. But a payment captured for a declined order is no longer refunded. This repo happens to have a model-checking unit test written for exactly this property, which also fails; the contract catches it without anyone having thought to write that test.

examples.title: A refactor believed equivalent that changes null handling
examples.summary: A nested switch was replaced by a one-line conditional. The agent that wrote it believed the two were equivalent, and every existing unit test passes. They differ on one input: a null status no longer throws.

examples.title: Logging a timestamp makes the decision unverifiable
examples.summary: Appending the current time to a reason string looks like harmless diagnostics. It makes the state machine depend on the clock, so its behaviour can no longer be proved, and the verifier refuses.

examples.title: An equivalent refactor passes without touching the contract
examples.summary: The same simplification as example 002, written with `default ->` instead of `==`. It really is equivalent, so the verifier proves it and the build passes.

examples.title: An intended change, reviewed as a one-line contract diff
examples.summary: Product asks for a clearer message when a customer cancels during payment. The developer changes the code and regenerates the contract, and the pull request shows exactly one changed outcome.

examples.title: A per-seat discount that rounds differently from the per-total one
examples.summary: The group discount is moved from the order total to the unit price, so that tickets can show what each seat cost. It reads as the same arithmetic, and the unit tests pass. The prover finds prices where the two versions differ by a few cents, over an input space of 2^96 values that no test could sweep.
notes: A one-cent rounding drift across 2^96 inputs: no type system and no sampled test can be relied on to find it.

examples.title: A doubled group discount, proved to change only groups
examples.summary: Product doubles the group discount from 10% to 20%. The developer declares that the change affects holds of six seats or more and nothing else, and the prover confirms it for every price and every smaller seat count. The pull request's claim becomes a checked fact.
examples.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: equivalent on every input outside the declared change
notes: Proves that a pricing change touches only the groups it says it touches, which is the claim a reviewer would otherwise take on trust.

examples.title: A new tier, written as one formula, also changes groups of six and seven
examples.summary: Product adds 20% off for eight seats or more. The developer writes it generally, a percentage per tier and one formula, and the pull request says that only eight seats or more are affected. The prover disagrees, and shows a group below eight seats whose price changed by a cent.

examples.title: A codec that loads whatever class a Kafka message names
examples.summary: To let one consumer decode messages of either family, the codec writes the Java class name into every payload and resolves it with Class.forName when reading. Round-trip tests pass. The module's capability contract now lists reflection, with the call site: the shape of the Jackson and XStream deserialization CVEs, caught without a CVE database.
notes: The codec starts loading classes named by Kafka messages: a deserialization gadget that a capability contract catches as one new capability.

examples.title: A codec setting that changes payloads but not what the module can do
examples.summary: Message properties are now written in alphabetical order, so that payloads in logs and dead-letter topics diff cleanly. The wire format changes, but the module reaches exactly the same JDK capabilities and libraries as before, and the capability contract passes untouched.

examples.title: Skipping one query in a Kafka listener strands a customer's money
examples.summary: When a payment is captured, the ticketing service counts the seats the order's hold still has before it decides. A developer removes that query: the hold was checked when the order was placed. No unit test covers the listener. The model checker finds a nine-step run across two customers, two services, Kafka and the clock after which a customer is charged, owns no seat, and the event that would have refunded them sits in a dead-letter topic.
notes: The Box Office model (`apps/boxoffice/spec`) has one action per service transaction, relay and clock tick, and TLC checks the README's safety invariants over every interleaving within small bounds. The order state machine in the model is generated from its B8 contract, so the model runs the proven bytecode behaviour.
The nine-step interleaving in which a paid customer loses both their seat and their refund.

examples.title: Deleting the hold sweeper, proved safe for every interleaving
examples.summary: The scheduled job that releases expired holds looks load-bearing: without it, seats of expired holds stay marked HELD. A developer deletes it anyway, and the model checker confirms that every safety invariant still holds in every reachable state, because the rest of the system already treats an expired hold as free.
examples.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: all invariants hold in 3,604 states
notes: The Box Office model (`apps/boxoffice/spec`) has one action per service transaction, relay and clock tick, and TLC checks the README's safety invariants over every interleaving within small bounds. The order state machine in the model is generated from its B8 contract, so the model runs the proven bytecode behaviour.

examples.title: A "longest log wins" vote rule lets a Raft leader overwrite committed entries
examples.summary: Raft's election restriction compares the last log entry's term first and its index second. A developer rewrites it the intuitive way round: the candidate with more entries has seen more history, so index first, term to break ties. Every unit test passes. The prover finds a voter and a candidate for which the old rule refuses the vote and the new one grants it, which is the configuration in which a leader can overwrite an entry the cluster already committed.
notes: A vote rule rewritten as "longest log wins" elects a leader that overwrites committed entries.

examples.title: A leader that ignores newer terms in replies keeps serving a term the cluster has left
examples.summary: Raft's rule for every server is one line: a message from a newer term makes you a follower. A developer narrows it for leaders, reasoning that a leader learns of a new term from the new leader's heartbeats, not from replies to its own RPCs. The behavioural contract of the role machine, 52 cases derived from the bytecode, changes in exactly one of them, and that one is the deposed-leader case.

examples.title: A majority rewritten as "half, rounded up" lets two quorums miss each other
examples.summary: The property that every quorum system rests on is that two majorities always share a node. The module states it next to the code, as `2 * majority(n) > n`, and the build proves it for every cluster size with a bounded model checker. A developer simplifies `n / 2 + 1` to `(n + 1) / 2`, which agrees on every odd size the tests use. The prover answers with n = 2: two "majorities" of one node each, which need not overlap.
notes: `(n + 1) / 2` is not a majority: two quorums of an even cluster can miss each other.

examples.title: A backoff cleanup that removes the overflow guard turns the delay negative
examples.summary: Exponential backoff is `min(cap, base << attempt)`, and the three lines that guard the shift against overflow look like paranoia, so a developer removes them. The module's properties file says a delay is never below the base, never above the cap, and never shorter than the previous attempt's. The prover finds an attempt count and a base for which the shift overflows into a negative delay, which a scheduler treats as "retry now", forever.

examples.title: A hybrid logical clock rewritten with max(), proved to never go backwards on any input
examples.summary: The receive rule of a hybrid logical clock has four branches; a developer rewrites it as one `max` and two conditionals. The property the clock exists for, that the new timestamp is later than both the last one and the message's and never behind the physical clock, is proved for every pair of 64-bit timestamps and every wall-clock reading. The refactor is merged on the strength of the proof, not of a review of the branches.
examples.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: property holds on every input

examples.title: A hybrid logical clock that drops one case stamps a receive before the message
examples.summary: The same rewrite as example 017, with the case where the last timestamp and the message share a physical part collapsed into the other two: continue whichever counter is checked first. The property that a receive event's timestamp is later than the message's is refuted with a message whose counter is ahead of the clock's. A transaction stamped with that clock would be ordered before an event it causally follows.
notes: With one branch folded away, the clock hands out a timestamp older than the message it just received.

examples.title: Adding jitter inside the backoff kernel gives a pure module a random number generator
examples.summary: The kernels in this module are pure so that a deterministic simulator can drive the whole cluster through thousands of seeded runs and replay any failure exactly. A developer adds jitter to the backoff, the textbook improvement, by calling `ThreadLocalRandom` inside the kernel, and updates the tests to accept a range. The module's capability contract, which lists every JDK capability its bytecode can reach, gains `randomness`, and the build fails: the module can no longer be replayed.

examples.title: A 2PC coordinator that presumes commit on timeout splits the participants
examples.summary: When the vote collection times out, the coordinator aborts: a participant that has not answered may have given up. A developer softens this: if every vote that did arrive was yes, the missing ones are slow, not opposed, so commit. The one-line contract diff is reviewed and approved. The model checker finds a three-step run in which a participant votes no, its vote is still in flight when the timer fires, "everyone who answered said yes" is true of nobody, and the coordinator commits a transaction that participant has already aborted.
notes: The two-phase-commit model (`apps/quorum/spec/TwoPhaseCommit.tla`) is built like Box Office's: the coordinator's state machine is generated from its B8 contract. An example of this model is checked under every configuration the model lists, and its verdict is the first that fails.
Commits over a participant's no vote that is still in flight.

examples.title: Aborting on the first no vote, proved safe for every interleaving of three participants
examples.summary: The coordinator used to wait for every vote before deciding, holding every participant's locks until the last straggler or the timeout. The developer makes it abort as soon as one no arrives. The regenerated contract changes in one case, the model checker runs every interleaving of three participants, the coordinator, the votes in flight and both timeouts, and every invariant holds in every state. The change is merged on a proof, not on a reviewer's mental model of the protocol.
examples.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: all invariants and properties hold in 644 states, and under 6 more configurations
notes: The two-phase-commit model (`apps/quorum/spec/TwoPhaseCommit.tla`) is built like Box Office's: the coordinator's state machine is generated from its B8 contract. An example of this model is checked under every configuration the model lists, and its verdict is the first that fails.

examples.title: A skew-tolerant tie-break for last-writer-wins lets replicas keep different values
examples.summary: Last-writer-wins resolution must be a total order on writes, or replicas that see the same two writes in different orders keep different values forever. The module states this as a law: `winner(a, b) == 1 - winner(b, a)` for distinct writes. A developer makes the tie-break tolerate clock skew, treating timestamps within five milliseconds as simultaneous and letting the node id decide. The prover finds two writes from the same node a couple of milliseconds apart that each replica resolves in favour of the one it saw first.

examples.title: A partitioner written with Math.abs sends one key in two billion to a negative partition
examples.summary: A custom Kafka partitioner routes a tenant's records by the hash of its id, so that every record of a tenant lands on the same partition. A developer rewrites Kafka's `toPositive(hash) % n`, with its unexplained bit mask, as `Math.abs(hash) % n`, which says what it means. The module's properties file says every hash lands on a partition of the topic. The prover finds the one `int` whose absolute value is negative, and the tool replays it: the partition is negative, which the producer rejects, and that tenant's records are never sent.
notes: `Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE)` is negative: one key in two billion goes to a negative partition.

examples.title: A JWT validator that applies clock skew on the wrong side rejects fresh tokens
examples.summary: A security review notes that the resource server accepts a token a few seconds before its `nbf`, and asks for that to stop. The developer moves the skew tolerance to the other side of the not-before check, so that a token is never accepted early. The module's properties file states two laws of a skew tolerance: it only ever widens acceptance, and a token is valid at every instant between its not-before and its expiry. The prover refutes both with a token checked a few seconds after it was issued, with a tolerance a little larger than that.

examples.title: A rollback rule rewritten as "unchecked means RuntimeException" commits after an Error
examples.summary: Spring's default rollback rule is that a `RuntimeException` or an `Error` rolls the transaction back and a checked exception does not. The kernel writes it as "anything but a checked exception", and a developer rewrites it in the positive, as "a runtime exception", which is how most people remember the rule. The behavioural contract of the transaction boundary, 22 cases derived from the bytecode, changes in exactly one: a method that dies with an `Error` now commits whatever it had written.
notes: Commits after an `OutOfMemoryError`: "a RuntimeException rolls back" is not "unchecked rolls back".

examples.title: A half-open circuit breaker that closes on the first good probe flaps through an outage
examples.summary: A half-open breaker lets a few probe calls through and closes only once all of them are back with the failure rate under the threshold. A developer, chasing the latency of the calls that queue behind the probes, makes the first successful probe enough to close. The behavioural contract of the breaker, 44 cases derived from the bytecode, changes in two of them, and the state-machine view drawn from the patched code shows HALF_OPEN with its waiting state gone.
notes: Compare 076, the half-open rule that judges probes by failure rate, and 075 and 077, the rules that keep every invariant and still never recover.

examples.title: A switch rewrite of the retry policy stops retrying the 5xx statuses it did not list
examples.summary: The retry policy is four `if` statements, and a developer rewrites them as one switch expression over the status, listing the retryable statuses by name, which reads better and is how the team now writes such tables. The regression proof compares the old and the new bytecode on every input, 2^96 of them, and finds a status in the five hundreds that the old code retried and the switch does not.
notes: The switch rewrite stops retrying the 5xx statuses it did not name.

examples.title: A retry helper that sleeps out the Retry-After delay gives a pure module a thread call
examples.summary: The kernels in this module decide and never wait: the retry policy returns whether to retry, and the client's scheduler does the waiting. A developer adds a convenience that waits out the server's `Retry-After` delay with `Thread.sleep` and then decides, so that a client filter can retry inline. The module's capability contract, which lists every JDK capability its bytecode can reach, gains `threads`, and the build fails: the module can now block the thread it is called on.

examples.title: An idempotency key that executes a retry while the first attempt is in flight pays twice
examples.summary: An `Idempotency-Key` receiver refuses a retry while the first attempt with that key is still in progress, with a 409. Support reports clients stuck in 409 loops after a worker died mid-request, and a developer makes the receiver run the retry instead: if a retry arrives, the first attempt is gone. The one-line contract diff is reviewed and approved. The model checker finds a five-step run in which the first attempt is not gone at all, and the request is executed twice.
notes: The idempotency model (`apps/crosscut/spec`) has a client retrying against an `Idempotency-Key` receiver whose state machine is generated from its contract.
An idempotency key that runs a retry while the first attempt is in flight executes the request twice.

examples.title: Storing a failed attempt's response under its key, proved at-most-once for every retry
examples.summary: The receiver used to release an idempotency key when the attempt under it died, so that the client's retry could run the request again. The developer makes it store the failure as the key's response instead, which is Stripe's semantics: a retry gets the first attempt's outcome, whatever it was. The regenerated contract changes in one case, the model checker runs every interleaving of three attempts against the new rule, and every invariant holds in every state. The change is merged on a proof, not on a reviewer's mental model of retries.
examples.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: all invariants hold in 131 states, and under 1 more configuration
notes: The idempotency model (`apps/crosscut/spec`) has a client retrying against an `Idempotency-Key` receiver whose state machine is generated from its contract.

examples.title: A token bucket that stamps each refill with "now" never refills under steady traffic
examples.summary: A token bucket's state is its tokens and the time up to which refills have been credited. The kernel advances that time by whole periods only, keeping the part of a period that has not earned a token yet. A developer simplifies it to "the refill happened now", which reads better and drops a remainder. The module's properties file says a refill never forgets a part of a period. The prover finds a refill short of a whole period, which the patched code credits anyway, and a bucket polled a little faster than it refills never earns a token again.

examples.title: A batch listener that commits the whole batch after a failed record loses the rest of it
examples.summary: A batch listener commits one past the last record it finished: the whole batch when every record is done, the failed record's own offset when one is not, so that it and everything after it come back. An on-call engineer, after a night of a consumer re-reading a poison batch, makes the listener commit the batch whatever happened, and updates the test to match. The module's properties file states what a committed offset means, and the prover refutes the change with a batch whose failed record is not its last.

examples.title: A cache expiry rewritten as a stored deadline, proved on every nanosecond and the sentinel
examples.summary: A cache's expire-after-write test is "has the time to live elapsed since the write". A developer rewrites it as "is now past the deadline", computing the deadline once at write time so that an eviction wheel can index entries by it, and guards the one addition that can overflow. The module's properties file says an entry expires exactly when its time to live has elapsed, and an entry that lives forever never does. The prover shows the rewrite satisfies it on all 2^192 inputs, including the `Long.MAX_VALUE` sentinel and the deadlines the addition cannot represent.
examples.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: property holds on every input

examples.title: An idiv that throws on Integer.MIN_VALUE / -1, where the JVM must return the dividend
examples.summary: The interpreter's `idiv` divides on the host and throws on a zero divisor, as the instruction does. A developer adds a second check: `Integer.MIN_VALUE / -1` is the one quotient an int cannot hold, so report it as an `ArithmeticException` too rather than return the wrong sign. The property the build proves of `idiv`, that dividing by -1 negates on every input, is refuted on exactly that input, with the exception as the outcome: JVMS §6.5 specifies the overflow and forbids the exception.
notes: Throws where the JVM specification says to return `Integer.MIN_VALUE`. Compare 053, the safe change on the same method.

examples.title: A NaN check written as == Float.NaN never fires, and fcmpl quietly becomes fcmpg
examples.summary: The interpreter's `fcmp` implements `fcmpg` and `fcmpl` with four branches: less, greater, equal, and the unordered case that the two opcodes decide differently. A developer moves the unordered case to the front, written as `a == Float.NaN || b == Float.NaN`, so that what follows is a plain three-way comparison. The regression proof against the previous version finds an input with a NaN on which `fcmpl` now pushes 1 instead of -1: a comparison with `Float.NaN` is false for every operand, including NaN.
notes: `== Float.NaN` is never true, so the NaN check never fires and `fcmpl` quietly becomes `fcmpg`.

examples.title: Switch lowering costs computed in int pick the wrong instruction for wide labels
examples.summary: The assembler chooses between `tableswitch` and `lookupswitch` with javac's heuristic: the table's space plus three times its time against the lookup's, computed in `long`. A developer drops the `long`: the costs are a few words and comparisons, and the casts clutter the formula. The regression proof against the previous version finds a label range on which the subtraction `hi - lo` overflows an `int`, and the two versions choose differently.

examples.title: tableSizeFor rewritten with numberOfLeadingZeros, proved equal on all 2^32 inputs
examples.summary: The symbol table rounds a requested capacity up to a power of two with the five-shift bit smear of JDK 8's `HashMap.tableSizeFor`. A developer replaces the smear with the one-line form JDK 11 adopted, `-1 >>> Integer.numberOfLeadingZeros(cap - 1)`. The regression proof compiles both versions into one program and proves them equal on every `int`, with the JDK's own bytecode of `numberOfLeadingZeros` in the proof.

examples.title: A verifier fast path for "everything is an Object" lets an uninitialized object pass
examples.summary: The type checker's assignability relation answers `isAssignable(from, to)` over the verification types, with the uninitialized types assignable to themselves and `top` only. A developer hoists the most frequent answer, that every reference is assignable to `Object`, above the rarer checks. The behavioural contract of the relation, 289 pairs derived from the bytecode, changes in two: `uninitialized` and `uninitializedThis` are now assignable to `Object`, which is the hole a type-checking verifier exists to close.
notes: The verifier answers "everything is an `Object`" one line too early, and an uninitialized object passes.

examples.title: Protected access without the receiver rule opens every superclass object to a subclass
examples.summary: Access control at resolution time admits a `protected` member from a subclass in another package only through an object of the subclass itself, as JVMS §5.4.4 requires in its "furthermore" clause. A developer drops the clause: a subclass inherits its superclass's protected members, and the receiver's type is the type checker's business. The behavioural contract of the check, 120 cases derived from the bytecode, changes in one: a protected instance member on an arbitrary object of the superclass is now accessible from a subclass in another package.

examples.title: Nest-based private access (JEP 181), reviewed as four lines of a 120-line contract
examples.summary: Access control admits a `private` member from its declaring class only; nestmates reach each other through the synthetic accessors javac generates. A developer implements JEP 181: a `private` member is also accessible from a class in the same nest. The behavioural contract is regenerated, and its diff is the four cases where the visibility is `private` and the relation is `same nest`, each `false` to `true`. The other 116 cases are proved unchanged, and the diff is what the reviewer approves.

examples.title: Looking up StrictMath intrinsics by name on the host gives a pure interpreter reflection
examples.summary: The interpreter computes a fixed list of the guest's `StrictMath` functions on the host, by a `switch` on the name. A developer replaces the list with a `MethodHandles.Lookup.findStatic` on the host's `StrictMath`, so that any unary function works without maintaining the list. The capability contract of the module, every capability `none` until now, gains `reflection` at two call sites: the interpreter can now invoke host methods chosen by a string, and the string comes from the guest's constant pool.

examples.title: Letting other threads proceed while <clinit> runs hands out a half-built class
examples.summary: A thread that needs a class another thread is initializing waits on the initialization lock, as step 2 of JVMS §5.5 says. Class-initialization deadlocks between classes whose initializers refer to each other are a known production problem, and a developer removes the wait: a request during initialization completes normally for every thread, as step 3 already allows for the initializing one. The contract diff is one line and is approved. The model checker finds a three-step run in which the second thread uses the class before its initializer has returned.
notes: The class initialization model (`apps/mica/spec`) has threads racing to initialize one class under the procedure of JVMS 5.5, and is checked for deadlock as well as for its invariants.

examples.title: One rule for every class-init request waits on its own thread, and TLC finds the deadlock
examples.summary: A request for a class being initialized waits, unless it comes from the initializing thread itself, which is a recursive request and completes normally (step 3 of JVMS §5.5). A developer removes the exception: every request during initialization waits, one rule, and the lock serializes everything. The contract diff is one line and is approved. The model checker, with deadlock detection on, finds a five-step run after which no thread can move: the initializer touched its own class, waited for itself, and every other thread waits for it.
notes: The class initialization model (`apps/mica/spec`) has threads racing to initialize one class under the procedure of JVMS 5.5, and is checked for deadlock as well as for its invariants.
One rule for every requester makes a thread wait on its own initialization: TLC's deadlock check finds it.

examples.title: A constant-pool encoder that writes NUL as one byte emits the byte no class file may hold
examples.summary: The class-file writer encodes `CONSTANT_Utf8_info` in modified UTF-8, where U+0000 takes two bytes so that no byte of an encoded string is zero. A developer aligns the encoder with standard UTF-8, one byte for every character up to U+007F, and updates the test that said otherwise. The property the build proves of the encoder, that no first byte is zero, is refuted on the one input it can be: the character U+0000, encoded as the byte 0, which JVMS §4.4.7 says no `CONSTANT_Utf8_info` may contain.

examples.title: A bisection midpoint written as (low + high) / 2, proved safe for every lookupswitch index
examples.summary: The interpreter bisects the sorted match-offset pairs of a `lookupswitch` with the midpoint `(low + high) >>> 1`, the idiom that survived the overflow bug in `Arrays.binarySearch`. A developer writes it as the division it is, `(low + high) / 2`. On every `int` that is the bug; on every index of a `lookupswitch` it is not, because a `Code` attribute holds at most 65535 bytes and a pair takes eight. The property committed for the midpoint carries that bound in its assumption, and the proof goes through; without the bound, the same proof fails in a fraction of a second.
examples.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: property holds on every input

examples.title: A lookupswitch bisection rewritten half-open, proved to find every key in a sorted table
examples.summary: The interpreter searches the sorted match-offset pairs of a `lookupswitch` by bisection, written the classic way: a closed range, two comparisons per step, three exits. A developer rewrites it in the half-open form, one comparison per step and one equality test at the end. The property committed for the search is its specification: on every strictly sorted table, the result is the index of the key when the key is in the table and -1 exactly when it is not, stated with JML's quantifiers over the array. The prover checks the rewritten bytecode against it on every sorted array up to the bound, and the proof goes through in a few seconds.
examples.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: property holds on every input
notes: The rewritten binary search still finds every key in every sorted table: a safe change, proved with quantifiers over the table.

examples.title: An exception table read with an inclusive end_pc hands an exception to the wrong handler
examples.summary: The interpreter finds the handler for a thrown exception in the `Code` attribute's exception table: the first entry, in table order, whose range covers the pc of the throwing instruction. The range is `[start_pc, end_pc)`, and the specification itself calls the exclusive end a historical mistake. A developer building a JVM decides not to repeat the mistake and makes the end inclusive, so that a handler can cover the last instruction of a method. The property the build proves of the lookup, stated over the table's columns as arrays, is refuted, and the counterexample is shrunk to a table of one entry whose `end_pc` is the pc of the throwing instruction, which the patched lookup hands to a handler that does not cover it.
notes: An `end_pc` read as inclusive hands an exception to the wrong handler. Compare 054, the check that compares `end_pc` like the other offsets.

examples.title: A constant-pool encoder that writes supplementary characters in four bytes, as UTF-8 does
examples.summary: The class-file writer encodes `CONSTANT_Utf8_info` in modified UTF-8, which has two differences from standard UTF-8: U+0000 takes two bytes, and a supplementary character is written as its two surrogates, three bytes each, never in the four-byte form. A developer who knows the second difference as CESU-8, the encoding every other tool deprecates, makes the encoder write the four-byte form for a surrogate pair, with a test for it. The property the build proves of the encoder is the sentence of JVMS §4.4.7 that forbids it: no byte of the encoding is zero, and none lies in `0xf0` to `0xff`. It is refuted on the first array that holds a surrogate pair.
notes: A regression proof of `ModifiedUtf8#encodeInto` is unfinished: proved up to 4 characters, it needs a machine with more memory at the default bound of 8 ([`apps/mica/pending`](../apps/mica/pending/README.md)).
Supplementary characters written in four bytes, as in standard UTF-8, produce a class no JVM will load.

examples.title: A stack map offset loop without the first-frame special case, proved to place every frame
examples.summary: A `StackMapTable` frame carries an `offset_delta`, not an offset: the first frame applies at `offset_delta`, every later one at the previous frame's offset plus `offset_delta + 1`. The class file reader's loop says so, with a special case for the first frame. A developer removes the special case by starting the count one byte before the code, so that every frame, the first included, is `offset_delta + 1` past the previous one. The property committed for the reader is the specification's own arithmetic, stated with JML's `\sum`, and a law stated with a call of the reader itself: no two frames share an offset. The prover checks the rewritten loop against both on every table up to the bound.
examples.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: property holds on every input
notes: With its first-frame special case removed, the stack map offset loop still places every frame: a safe change.

examples.title: A Code attribute length that omits the nested attributes' headers truncates the method
examples.summary: The writer of a class file computes the `attribute_length` of a `Code` attribute: twelve fixed bytes, the code, eight per exception table entry, and the nested attributes, each a six-byte header followed by its own `attribute_length` bytes. A developer reads in JVMS §4.7 that an attribute's length does not include its initial six bytes, and makes the loop add each nested attribute's length and nothing else. The property committed for the computation, stated with JML's `\sum` over the nested lengths, is refuted at once; the counterexample JBMC finds is an eight-attribute table of large numbers, which the tool shrinks in its interpreter to one nested attribute of length zero, six bytes short.
notes: The array refutations of these Mica kernels are shrunk to a witness of one element.
Six bytes short per nested attribute: the headers are left out of the `Code` attribute's length.

examples.title: A constant-pool index that counts the long entry itself points one past the entry
examples.summary: Constant pool entries are numbered from 1, and a `CONSTANT_Long` or `CONSTANT_Double` entry takes two numbers, the one after it being unusable: the specification calls this, in retrospect, a poor choice. The class file reader maps an entry's position to its number by walking the entries before it. A developer rewrites the walk as a count of the two-number entries, and counts up to and including the entry itself. The property committed for the mapping, stated with JML's `\num_of`, is refuted on a pool of one long constant, whose number comes out as 2 instead of 1.
notes: The array refutations of these Mica kernels are shrunk to a witness of one element.
The numbering counts the `long` entry itself, which takes two slots, and points one past it.

examples.title: A max_stack that checks the depth only after a push, proved to find the deepest point
examples.summary: The assembler computes `max_stack` for a `Code` attribute: the deepest the operand stack gets, which for a straight-line sequence is the largest running sum of the instructions' stack effects. The loop compares the depth with the maximum after every instruction. A developer compares it only after an instruction that pushes more than it pops, since no other instruction can leave the stack deeper than it was. The property committed for the computation is the definition itself, `\max` over the prefix sums, written as nested JML quantifiers, under the assumption that the effects are those of JVM instructions. The prover checks the changed loop against it on every such sequence up to the bound; stated over every `int` effect instead, the same property refutes the change, on two effects whose sum wraps, which is the premise the developer's argument did not state.
examples.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: property holds on every input
notes: The array refutations of these Mica kernels are shrunk to a witness of one element.
`max_stack` is still the deepest point when the depth is checked only after a push: a safe change.

examples.title: An idiv that leaves division by zero to the host, proved to throw exactly there
examples.summary: The interpreter's `idiv` checks for a zero divisor and throws `ArithmeticException` before dividing on the host. A developer notices that the host is itself a JVM, whose division throws the same exception on the same input, and removes the check from `idiv` and `irem`. The property committed for each kernel now declares the exceptional behaviour as JML does, `throws: ArithmeticException when divisor == 0`, instead of assuming the zero divisor away; the prover covers the exceptional path with the normal one and proves that the host throws exactly where the check did.
examples.verdictLabel: ✓ Verified: property holds on every input
notes: The throws clause of the property brings the exceptional path under the proof.
Leaving division by zero to the host throws exactly where the removed check did. Compare 034, the unsafe change on the same method.

examples.title: An exception table check that rejects a handler range ending at code_length
examples.summary: The class file reader checks each exception table entry as JVMS §4.7.3 requires: `start_pc` before `end_pc`, `end_pc` at most `code_length`, `handler_pc` inside the code. A developer makes the three offsets uniform, all of them less than `code_length`, reasoning that an offset into the code is an offset into the code. The property committed for the check is a throws clause, the specification's three conditions as the condition under which the reader throws `ClassFormatError`; the prover refutes the uniform check on the smallest method there is, one byte of code covered by a handler that ends where the code ends, which the patched reader rejects as malformed.
notes: The throws clause of the property brings the exceptional path under the proof.
Rejects every handler that covers the last instruction of a method, since `end_pc == code_length` is allowed.

examples.title: An encoder that zero-terminates the string into the caller's buffer
examples.summary: `encodeInto` writes the modified UTF-8 encoding of a `char[]` into a buffer the caller provides and returns how many bytes it wrote. A developer adds a zero byte after the encoding when the buffer has room, so that the bytes can be handed to native code as a C string, which is what the encoding's zero-free form exists for. The property committed for the encoder now has a frame condition in JML's `\old`: the bytes past what it wrote are as the call received them. The prover refutes the patched encoder on an empty string and a one-byte buffer, whose byte it zeroes.
notes: A regression proof of `ModifiedUtf8#encodeInto` is unfinished: proved up to 4 characters, it needs a machine with more memory at the default bound of 8 ([`apps/mica/pending`](../apps/mica/pending/README.md)).
Writes one byte past what it returns into the caller's buffer, refuted against a frame condition stated with JML's `\old`.

examples.title: A lookupswitch pair sort that compares keys by difference
examples.summary: The assembler sorts the match-offset pairs of a `lookupswitch` by key, as JVMS §6.5 requires, with an insertion sort that keeps each offset with its key. A developer factors the comparison into a `compare` method that returns the difference of the two keys, the comparator idiom. The property committed for the sort says that the keys come out sorted and that every pair the call received is among the pairs it left, in JML's `\old`. The prover refutes the patched sort on two keys in order whose difference overflows, `Integer.MIN_VALUE + 271` and `272`, which it swaps.
notes: Comparing keys by difference overflows and swaps two keys just over 2^31 apart, refuted against a permutation stated with JML's `\old`.

examples.title: A coordinator that waits for the last vote when every vote so far is yes blocks forever
examples.summary: When the vote collection times out, the two-phase-commit coordinator aborts: a participant that has not answered may have given up. A developer makes it keep collecting instead when every vote that did arrive was yes, so as not to throw away a transaction every responder approved. Every safety invariant of the protocol model still holds, and so does the contract diff the reviewer approves. The model's liveness property, that every participant eventually decides, does not: TLC shows a six-step run after which two prepared participants hold their locks forever.
notes: The two-phase-commit model (`apps/quorum/spec/TwoPhaseCommit.tla`) is built like Box Office's: the coordinator's state machine is generated from its B8 contract. An example of this model is checked under every configuration the model lists, and its verdict is the first that fails.

This configuration states fairness conditions and a liveness property (every participant eventually decides), and checks that the model implements Lamport and Gray's transaction-commit specification, a refinement TLC checks step by step.

Waiting for the last vote when every vote so far is yes leaves a prepared participant holding its locks forever: a liveness failure no invariant and no deadlock check can state, found under the model's fairness conditions.

examples.title: A grace period for the last vote, proved to keep every participant deciding
examples.summary: The developer of example 057 tries again: when the collection times out with every vote so far yes, the coordinator moves to a new phase, `GRACE`, and waits one more period; a second timeout aborts. The contract gains a phase and seven cases, and the model's guard on the timer, its type invariant and its inductive invariant gain the phase. TLC checks the invariants, the liveness property that every participant eventually decides, and that the protocol still implements Lamport and Gray's transaction commit specification, and all of them hold in every state and every behaviour; and the inductive step holds too, so atomicity is proved for the new protocol by induction, not only by search.

examples.title: A server that grants a vote without adopting the candidate's term elects two leaders
examples.summary: A Raft server that receives a vote request from a newer term adopts the term and becomes a follower of it, and only then applies the vote rule. A developer stops the adoption, so that a server whose timer fired cannot drag the cluster into a new term by asking: the vote rule already counts a candidate's newer term as a free vote, so the vote is still granted. The contract diff is three cases, one per role, and is approved; the vote rule is untouched and its regression proofs pass. The election model finds a five-step run that ends with two leaders in one term.
notes: The Raft election model (`apps/quorum/spec/RaftElection.tla`) is built around the role machine, generated from its contract, with election safety as an invariant and two action properties, `[][A]_v` formulas that constrain each step: terms never decrease, a leader never campaigns. An example is checked under all of the model's configurations, and its verdict is the first that fails.
A bug in how two kernels compose: each kernel's own contract approves it, and only the model of the two together finds two leaders.

examples.title: One timeout rule for every role makes a leader campaign against itself
examples.summary: A follower or candidate whose election timer fires becomes a candidate of the next term; a leader's timer firing is ignored, since a leader holds no elections. A developer folds the two cases into one: every server runs for office when its timer fires, and the leader's case was dead code because the timer is stopped when a server wins. The contract diff is one case and is approved. Every invariant of the election model holds, because a candidate of term 2 is an ordinary state. The action property that a leader never becomes a candidate does not: TLC shows the four-step run in which a leader deposes itself.

An example is checked under all of the model's configurations, and its verdict is the first that fails.
One timeout rule for every role makes a leader resign into an election against itself.

examples.title: A leader that steps down when its timer fires, proved to keep one leader per term
examples.summary: A Raft leader cut off from the majority keeps believing it leads, and keeps serving reads from a state the rest of the cluster has moved past, until some message from the newer term reaches it. A developer adds the check etcd calls CheckQuorum: a leader whose election timer fires, meaning no majority acknowledged it for a whole timeout, steps down to follower. The contract diff is one case and is approved. The election model proves the change keeps every invariant and both action properties, in 1,153 states: one leader per term, terms that never go backwards, and no leader that campaigns.

examples.title: A candidate that retries its election without voting for itself again elects two leaders
examples.summary: A Raft candidate whose election timed out starts a new one: a new term, a vote for itself, a request to every other server. A developer trims the retry: the tally already holds the candidate's own vote, so it need not vote again, and the request goes only to the servers that never answered. The contract diff is one case and is approved. The election model finds the bug under each of its three safety configurations, each in its own way: a seven-step run of three servers in which two candidates elect each other, the one step that breaks the inductive invariant (a candidate of a term it has not voted in), and an eight-step run of four servers in which a vote cast in term 1 is counted in term 2.

examples.title: A candidate that retries in the same term, proved safe, and shown never to elect a leader
examples.summary: A Raft candidate whose election timed out starts a new one in a new term. A developer makes it ask again in the same term instead, for the votes it lacks, so that a candidate that cannot win does not drive the whole cluster's term up on every timeout. The contract diff is one case and is approved. The election model proves the change safe under three of its configurations: one leader per term, with three servers, by induction, and with four. The fourth configuration, the liveness check, finds the run the safety proofs cannot see: three servers whose timers fire together are three candidates of term 1, each refused by the other two, and under this rule nothing ever starts term 2. The cluster has no leader, for good. A green safety result says exactly what it checked; the liveness property says the rest.
notes: The Raft election model (`apps/quorum/spec/RaftElection.tla`) is built around the role machine, generated from its contract, with election safety as an invariant and two action properties, `[][A]_v` formulas that constrain each step: terms never decrease, a leader never campaigns. An example is checked under all of the model's configurations, and its verdict is the first that fails.

`RaftElectionLive.cfg` checks liveness under fairness: a timer nothing resets fires, a candidate asks for the votes it lacks, a leader sends its heartbeats. Each action's enabling condition is written out as a state predicate, so that TLC need not compute `ENABLED` on every step of the liveness check. A retry rule can keep every safety property and still break liveness.
Proved safe under every safety configuration, yet three candidates ask each other forever: a liveness failure only the fairness configuration can state. Compare 064.

examples.title: A candidate that stands down on a timeout, proved safe and live
examples.summary: A Raft candidate whose election timed out starts a new one at once. A developer makes it stand down to follower instead, so that its next timeout, after a full randomized wait, starts the new election: a split vote is then retried by its candidates one at a time rather than all together. The contract diff is one case and is approved. The election model proves the change under all four of its configurations: one leader per term with three servers, by induction, and with four, and under fairness a run that stays within the term budget still elects a leader, and a leader the cluster has left behind still steps down. The liveness check is the one a reviewer wants for a rule that makes candidates stand down: the question is whether the election can stall, and the answer is no, because a follower's timer starts a new term.

examples.title: A leader that ignores vote requests from newer terms votes twice in a term
examples.summary: A Raft server that hears a newer term from anyone becomes a follower of that term. A developer exempts the leader from the vote request: a leader should keep serving until a newer leader's heartbeat, or a reply from a newer term, proves the cluster has moved on, so that a server that comes back from a partition with an inflated term cannot depose a working leader on every retry. The contract diff is one case and is approved. The election model finds the bug under all three of its safety configurations: an eight-step run of three servers in which the leader's vote elects two candidates of the same term, the one step that breaks the inductive invariant (a leader that holds a vote cast in an older term), and a longer run of four servers.

An example is checked under all of the model's configurations, and its verdict is the first that fails.

examples.title: A leader that treats a vote request of its own term as impossible crashes on a split vote
examples.summary: The Raft role machine throws on one input, a leader hearing a leader of its own term, because election safety says it cannot happen. A developer extends the reasoning to vote requests: a candidate campaigning in a term that already has a leader is just as impossible, so a leader throws on a vote request of its own term too. The contract diff is one case, from unchanged to an exception, and is approved; the input is covered by a new test, which checks that it throws. The election model has an invariant for exactly this claim, that no input the protocol can deliver makes the role machine throw, and it fails in four steps: two servers time out into term 1, one wins with the third's vote, and the other, still a candidate of term 1, asks the new leader for its vote. A split vote makes the exception reachable, and the leader crashes on the loser's request.
notes: The Raft election model (`apps/quorum/spec/RaftElection.tla`) is built around the role machine, generated from its contract, with election safety as an invariant and two action properties, `[][A]_v` formulas that constrain each step: terms never decrease, a leader never campaigns. An example is checked under all of the model's configurations, and its verdict is the first that fails.
The invariant that no reachable state lets the generated kernel throw (`KernelNeverThrows`) turns the kernel's `IllegalStateException`, a claim that an input never occurs, into a checked theorem.
The exception is dead for the one input the kernel already threw on, and reachable in four steps for the new one, the loser of a split vote.

examples.title: A coordinator that commits after aborting on timeout, once the late votes are all yes
examples.summary: When the vote collection times out, the two-phase-commit coordinator aborts: a participant that has not answered may have given up. A developer adds a second chance: if the missing votes arrive after all and every one of them is yes, the abort was a wrong guess and nothing has been lost, so the coordinator commits. The contract diff is one case, in the `ABORTED` phase, and is approved; the test that said an aborted transaction stays aborted is adjusted to the new rule. The model finds the run the developer did not picture in nine steps, and the inductive step finds it in one: an abort is a decision participants act on, and by the time the late votes are in, a participant that voted yes has aborted on the coordinator's say-so and released its locks. The commit that follows splits the participants.
notes: The two-phase-commit model (`apps/quorum/spec/TwoPhaseCommit.tla`) is built like Box Office's: the coordinator's state machine is generated from its B8 contract. An example of this model is checked under every configuration the model lists, and its verdict is the first that fails.

`TwoPhaseCommitInductive.cfg` checks an inductive invariant, four conjuncts about the votes counted and in flight, from every state it admits: it proves atomicity by induction and finds a wrong second decision in one step.
Found as a nine-step run and as the one step that leaves the inductive invariant. Compare 068, proved safe both ways.

examples.title: A coordinator that answers a late vote with its decision, proved to keep every decision
examples.summary: A vote that reaches the coordinator after it has decided comes from a participant that may not have heard the decision, and a prepared participant holds its locks until it does. The developer makes the coordinator answer every late vote by sending its decision again. The contract diff is eight cases, every tally in a decided phase, from unchanged to a transition that stays in the phase and resends. The model proves the change keeps every decision: the same 728 states as before, every invariant and property holding, and the inductive step, which ties what the coordinator broadcasts to the phase it is in, closed under the new rule. Example 067 is the same eight rows done wrong.

examples.title: A vote rule that lets a voter switch candidates within a term elects two leaders
examples.summary: Raft's vote rule grants one vote per term: a server that has voted for a candidate refuses every other candidate of that term, and a split vote costs the cluster a new term. A developer lets the vote move instead: a candidate still asking in the voter's term is one the term's election has not settled, since the candidate the voter chose has not won, so the vote goes to whoever is asking and the split resolves within the term. The behavioural contract of the vote rule, a second operator of the election model generated from the Java, changes in three rows, and the tests are updated to say so. TLC finds two leaders of one term in five steps: two servers time out together, and each, still a candidate, grants the other its vote. The vote a server cast for itself moves too, and both tallies reach a majority.
notes: The Raft election model (`apps/quorum/spec/RaftElection.tla`) is built around the role machine, generated from its contract, with election safety as an invariant and two action properties, `[][A]_v` formulas that constrain each step: terms never decrease, a leader never campaigns. An example is checked under all of the model's configurations, and its verdict is the first that fails.

The vote rule is the election model's second generated operator, brought in as an `INSTANCE`, and `RaftElectionLogs.cfg` gives one server the log a deposed leader left behind, which a leader elected without the election restriction would overwrite.
Letting a voter switch candidates to settle split votes faster elects two leaders that hold each other's votes.

examples.title: A vote rule without the election restriction elects a leader missing a committed entry
examples.summary: Raft's vote rule refuses a candidate whose log is behind the voter's, the election restriction, so that a leader never lacks a committed entry. A developer drops it for the approach of Viewstamped Replication, in which the new primary collects the log from a majority after it is chosen: the vote need not wait for the candidate with the best log, since a leader that lacks entries will fetch them before it serves. The contract of the vote rule changes in five rows, and the tests are updated to say so. The election model's four configurations with equal logs verify the change; the fifth, in which one server holds the log a deposed leader left behind, longer than the others' and of an older term, finds in three steps that this server is elected with one vote besides its own, lacking the entry the other two hold and have therefore committed. A Raft leader never collects entries: it makes the followers' logs match its own, and the committed entry would be overwritten.

examples.title: A vote rule that compares log length before term grants a vote it must refuse
examples.summary: The election model checks the vote rule's decision kernel, generated from its contract, and repeats the arithmetic around it: how the candidate's term and log compare with the voter's own is computed in `grant`, outside the model's reach. A developer reorders that comparison so that the longer log wins and the term of the last entry breaks ties between logs of one length, reading "up to date" as "further along". The kernel's contract does not change and the election model verifies it under every configuration, logs included, since the model does its own comparing. The property that states the election restriction over `grant` itself, that a candidate whose last entry is of an older term is refused however long its log, fails: JBMC shows a voter whose last entry is of a later term granting a candidate whose log is longer but ends in an earlier one, the log a deposed leader left behind. examples.title: A vote rule that refuses a repeat request is verified by a model that never asks twice
examples.summary: Raft's vote rule grants a candidate the vote it already holds: a server votes once per term, and the candidate that has the vote may ask again, because the reply that carried it may have been lost. A developer reads one vote per term literally and refuses the repeat, as a duplicate the tally must not count twice; the contract of the vote rule changes in two rows, and the tests are updated to say so. The election model verifies the change under all five configurations, and for the first time the verdict comes with what it rests on: TLC's coverage of the generated operator, read back row by row by the tool, shows that no run of the model takes either row the change alters. The model's RPCs are atomic, a request and its reply in one step, so no candidate ever asks a voter twice, and the rows for a repeat are dead in it. The verdict is vacuous, and the tool says so.

examples.title: A follower that leads on a late majority passes a model that never counts votes late
examples.summary: Raft's role machine ignores a tally counted by a server that is no longer a candidate: the votes are of an election the server has left. A developer lets a follower that finds a majority in its tally take the leadership, reasoning that a candidate which stepped down while its votes were in flight was elected all the same; the contract changes in one row the model can see, and a test says so. The election model verifies the change under all five configurations, and coverage shows that no run takes the row: in the model a vote is counted in the step that grants it, by the candidate itself, and a server that steps down in that step empties its tally first, so there is no late majority to count. The verdict is vacuous, and the tool says so. In a cluster the late votes are of the term the server left: a candidate of term 1 that heard the leader of term 2, stepped down, and then counted its term-1 majority would lead term 2 beside its leader.

examples.title: A coordinator that aborts the transaction on restart reverses a commit it had sent
examples.summary: A two-phase-commit coordinator logs each phase change before it acts on it, and a restart after a crash reads the log: a logged decision is sent again, since the crash may have come before the broadcast, and no logged decision means abort. A developer collapses the three cases of the recovery rule into one, abort: whatever the coordinator was doing, an abort releases the participants' locks, and a transaction that was about to commit can be retried. The contract diff is one row, a restart in `COMMITTED`, from sending the commit again to aborting. The two-phase-commit model is now checked under two more configurations, in which the coordinator may crash between steps or between logging a decision and sending it, and restarts on the recovery rule, generated from the contract like the decision rule. Under the two the model had, nothing crashes and the row is never taken. Under the third, TLC finds in ten steps a commit that is sent, applied by one participant, and then reversed by the restarted coordinator, which tells the other two to abort; the fourth finds the same step from a state its inductive invariant admits.
notes: The two-phase-commit model (`apps/quorum/spec/TwoPhaseCommit.tla`) is built like Box Office's: the coordinator's state machine is generated from its B8 contract. An example of this model is checked under every configuration the model lists, and its verdict is the first that fails.

`TwoPhaseCommitCrash.cfg` and `TwoPhaseCommitCrashInductive.cfg` let the coordinator crash between steps, or after logging a decision and before sending it, and restart on a recovery rule, the model's second generated operator (`Recovery#decide`).

Under the two configurations the model had, nothing crashes and the rows are never taken; the inductive invariant is closed under the new rule as well, since every state the run passes through is one it admits. The two prepared participants hold their locks forever, a liveness failure, reported as a run that stays in its last state. The fourth configuration finds the step that makes it possible, a coordinator up and decided with nothing out.

examples.title: An Idempotency-Key header added to POST /orders drops the request body's validation on the way
examples.summary: Clients already send an `Idempotency-Key` on `POST /concerts/{id}/holds`, so a developer makes `POST /orders` accept the same header, writing the handler's new parameter list by hand. The module's boundary contract, the routes and the advice on each read from the compiled classes, shows the `POST /orders` line changing from a validated body to an unvalidated one, next to the header that was added.
notes: The first example of approach B12, the boundary contract (`jvmcontract boundaries`, `verify --add boundaries`): where Spring enters a module and the advice on each bean, from the annotations in the class files. The three Box Office modules with Spring annotations carry theirs in `src/contract/boundaries.contract`, checked by `./gradlew check` when `jvmcontract` is on the PATH (`verifyBoundaries`, `updateBoundaries`).

Box Office keeps its transactions programmatic (`Transactions`), so none of the contract's `!` lines (self-invocation of a `@Transactional` method, advice on a private or final method, a checked exception that commits, a lost `@Async` result) occur here; the library's Spring fixtures (`lib/tests/fixtures/spring`) have one of each. An example of a `@Transactional` self-invocation needs a service with `@Transactional` beans: a candidate for Crosscut's framework glue, which the kernels there deliberately leave out.

The runner (`build.py`, `run_boundaries`) compiles the patched module with Gradle and runs `jvmcontract verify` over its `src/contract` directory; it does not use the Gradle build's own `verifyBoundaries` task, so it works without the tool on the PATH of the Gradle daemon. The existing tests are the module's Spring Boot tests, which need Docker for Testcontainers; without it they fail before the change is tested, which the page records as the tests' result, not the verifier's.

examples.title: A PaymentVoided event joins the sealed PaymentEvent family without its @JsonSubTypes entry
examples.summary: The payment service voids an order whose refund arrives before any charge, and until now told nobody. A developer adds a `PaymentVoided` record to the sealed `PaymentEvent` interface, publishes it on the void path, and handles it in ticketing, where the compiler insists on the new case of the sealed switch. The `@JsonSubTypes` list on the interface, which names the type id of each event on the wire, is not touched. Every test passes: the compiler checked the Java side, the codec test round-trips the three events it knew about. Jackson writes the new event with the type id `PaymentEvent$PaymentVoided` and the consumer rejects it. The regenerated boundary contract of the `contracts` module shows the new type with a `!` line saying exactly that.
notes: The first example of the wire types in a boundary contract (`jvmcontract boundaries`, `verify --add boundaries`): the JSON shape of each request, response and message type as Jackson encodes it, with `!` lines for the Jackson pitfalls that no test with the same classes on both sides can see. The `contracts` module of Box Office has no Spring annotations; its boundary contract is wire types only, and it is checked by `./gradlew check` like the others when `jvmcontract` is on the `PATH`.

The runner (`build.py`, `run_boundaries`) treats an intended change as a regeneration: it runs `jvmcontract update`, records the contract diff, and reports as the violation any `!` line the regenerated contract has that the old one did not. An unintended change is a plain `verify`, as in example 110.

Jackson 3.1 behaviour, checked with a scratch program against the jars Box Office uses: a permitted subtype missing from an explicit `@JsonSubTypes` is written as `Outer$Inner` and rejected on reading; a sealed interface with `@JsonTypeInfo` and no `@JsonSubTypes` accepts all permitted subtypes under their class names, which the contract reports as a type id that is a class name; a listed subtype without `name` gets the class name too. Jackson 2 does not read permitted subclasses at all, so there the unlisted event fails on reading in every case.

The patch touches three modules (the record, the publisher, the consumer's switch); the runner compiles and checks the `contracts` module, where the subject is. The payment-service tests that exercise the void path are not in this patch, as they were not in the developer's change.

examples.title: A prod profile raises the hold seat limit under boxoffice.hold.max-seat, a key nothing reads

The other `!` lines of the block, each in the library's Spring fixtures (`lib/tests/fixtures/spring/resources/application.yaml`): a key the metadata marks deprecated (`spring.data.mongodb.uri` in Spring Boot 4, which no longer binds it and names `spring.mongodb.uri`), a value that is not of the key's type (`ttl: 2 minutes` for a `Duration`, `port: eighty`, an enum constant that does not exist), and a placeholder default that is not (`${holds.retries:many}` for an `int`). The patch changes no Java, so the module compiles as before and the existing tests pass as before; the runner compiles it anyway, since the contract is read from the classes and the files together. The Spring Boot tests of the module need Docker for Testcontainers; without it they fail before the change is tested, which the page records as the tests' result, not the verifier's.

examples.title: A nested Billing record on PlaceOrder carries @NotBlank constraints that no @Valid leads into

The patch changes the Java of the module, so the runner compiles it with Gradle, reads the runtime class path through the build's `printRuntimeClasspath` task, and runs `jvmcontract update` then `verify` with `--resources` and `--classpath`. examples.title: GET /holds/{id} now extends the hold it returns: a polling checkout page keeps seats held for ever
examples.summary: The developer makes `GET /holds/{id}` keep the hold alive: `HoldService.get` pushes the expiry of the hold and of its seats forward on every call, so a customer filling in the payment form does not lose the seats under them. The checkout page polls that endpoint for its countdown, so a hold now never expires while a tab is open, a browser's prefetch or a monitor's probe keeps seats off the market, and a retried GET changes state. The boundary contract now says what each entry point reaches (the documents it reads and writes, the topics it sends to, the HTTP calls it makes, the events it publishes); the regenerated contract has `writes HoldDocument, SeatDocument` under the GET and a `!` line: a safe method with side effects.
notes: The first example of the reach lines of a boundary contract (`lib/src/reach.rs`). For every entry point and advised method, the tool follows the calls in the bytecode through the application's own classes (the module and its sibling modules on the class path; a call into Spring, the JDK or a driver is a leaf) and classifies the leaves: the Spring Data templates and repositories, the JPA `EntityManager` and `JdbcTemplate` give `reads` and `writes` (of the class literal passed, else the static type of the entity argument, else the documents the method mentions; a table from the SQL constant), the Kafka, RabbitMQ, JMS and Spring Cloud Stream templates give `sends` (the topic when it is a constant, else `to Kafka`), `RestTemplate`, `RestClient`, `WebClient` and `@HttpExchange` or Feign interfaces give `calls GET /path`, `ApplicationEventPublisher` gives `publishes`. A virtual call goes to every local subtype that overrides the method, a lambda to its body whether or not the receiver runs it: a may-reach approximation, which is the right side to err on for a reviewer.

Two checks read these lines: a `GET` or `HEAD` route that writes, sends, publishes or makes a non-GET call is `! a GET that ...: a safe method with side effects`, and a `@Transactional(readOnly = true)` method that writes is `! @Transactional(readOnly = true) but writes ...: a read-only transaction drops or rejects writes` (Hibernate sets the flush mode to manual and silently keeps the changes, PostgreSQL rejects the statement, MongoDB ignores the flag). The Box Office contracts regenerated with reach lines under every route, listener and schedule and no `!` line: `POST /orders` reads `HoldDocument, OrderDocument, SeatDocument` and writes `OrderDocument, Outbox.Entry`, the payment listener reads `Inbox.Entry, OrderDocument, SeatDocument` and writes those plus `Outbox.Entry`, the outbox relay in the messaging module `sends to Kafka` (the topic is read from the entry, so it is not a constant). A nested class keeps its outer name so the two `Entry` records stay apart.

What the lines do not say: the order of the effects, the condition under which each happens (the write here runs only while the hold is unexpired; the line says `writes`), or anything a framework does on the module's behalf (a `@Transactional` commit, a Kafka offset commit, an audit aspect). A method called through reflection or a bean looked up by name is not followed; a data call whose entity argument is a `List` built elsewhere falls back to the documents the method mentions. The GET check is a statement about HTTP semantics, not about this application: a GET that records a metric or refreshes a cache is flagged the same way, and the line is for the reviewer to accept or move.

The change is a feature rather than a refactoring because the keep-alive is what the developer wants; the point of the example is that the contract puts the cost of the shortcut on the page the reviewer reads, as a side effect of a safe method, instead of leaving it to be found when the next concert sells out with half the seats held by abandoned tabs. examples.title: Payment command sent to Kafka from inside the order transaction: the outbox dropped for a dual write
examples.summary: The developer drops the outbox from the order path: `OrderService.place` sends the `ChargePayment` command to Kafka itself, from inside the MongoDB transaction that records the order, so the payment service hears about the order at once instead of on the relay's next poll. The send is not part of the transaction. A write conflict makes `Transactions.run` retry the work, and each attempt sends a fresh command with a fresh id; a transaction that rolls back after the send has told the payment service to charge for an order that does not exist; a process that dies between the commit and the send leaves an order that waits for a payment nobody was asked for. The boundary contract places every effect with respect to transactions; the regenerated contract has `sends payments.commands` under `POST /orders` and a `!` line: a transaction that sends.
notes: The first example of the transaction placement of the reach lines (`lib/src/reach.rs`): the walk from each entry point carries a scope, outside any transaction, inside one the root opened, or inside a `@Transactional` method of another class, and the effects go into `all`, `outside` and `inside` sets. The root is inside its own transaction when it is `@Transactional` (with a propagation that joins or opens one); a lambda enters the root's transaction when it is an argument of a call to `TransactionTemplate.execute` or `executeWithoutResult`, or to a method (a runner) that reaches either of those or a `@Transactional` method: Box Office's `Transactions.run(Supplier)` calls `template.execute`, and `run(Runnable)` calls that, so a lambda handed to either is inside. A `@Transactional` method of another class on the path takes its effects for itself (its own member in the contract carries them), so the `!` line sits under the service method and not under every route that calls it; a `@Transactional` method of the same class is a self-invocation, which the proxy does not see, and changes nothing.

examples.title: Hold route variable renamed in the template but not in the parameter: a 500 on every request of it
examples.summary: The developer renames the path variable of `GET /holds/{id}` to `{holdId}`, so the route reads like the OpenAPI description, and leaves the handler's parameter as `@PathVariable String id`. Spring binds a `@PathVariable` by name, the annotation's or the parameter's, at request time: no template of the route has a variable named `id`, so every request of the route ends in `MissingPathVariableException`, a 500. The code compiles, the context starts, and the module's unit tests, which call the service and not the route, pass. The boundary contract now checks each handler's request binding; the regenerated contract has a `!` line under the renamed route: `@PathVariable id matches no variable in /holds/{holdId}`.
notes: The first example of the request binding checks (`lib/src/binding.rs`), which read a handler's parameter annotations against its routes and its bytecode. A `@PathVariable`, `@RequestParam`, `@RequestHeader`, `@CookieValue` or `@MatrixVariable` binds by name: the annotation's `value` or `name`, else the parameter's name as the `MethodParameters` attribute records it (what `javac -parameters` writes and what Spring reads by reflection; the `LocalVariableTable` of `-g`, which Spring 6.0 fell back to, is not read by 6.1). The pattern key drops the variable names and the constraints inside the braces; `consumes`, `produces`, `params` and `headers` stay in the key, so two routes that differ in them are not reported (Spring tells them apart by the request's headers). The Box Office contracts regenerated unchanged: every `@PathVariable` of the three modules names a variable of its route, the modules compile with `-parameters`, and no two handlers share a pattern.

examples.title: HoldExpiredException replaces the ConflictException and no handler maps it: a 500 instead of a 409
examples.summary: The developer gives the expired-hold case of `POST /orders` its own exception, `HoldExpiredException`, carrying the hold id, so that callers and logs can tell it from the other conflicts, and leaves `ApiErrors`, the `@RestControllerAdvice`, as it was. The new class extends `RuntimeException`, not `ConflictException`, so no `@ExceptionHandler` takes it and no `@ResponseStatus` marks it: a client that places an order for an expired hold now gets a 500 from the container's error page instead of the 409 problem detail. The code compiles, the context starts, and the module's unit tests, which call the service and not the route, pass. The boundary contract now lists under each route what it throws and what each exception becomes; the regenerated contract has a `!` line under `POST /orders`: `throws HoldExpiredException: no @ExceptionHandler takes it and it carries no @ResponseStatus, so the response is a 500`.
notes: The first example of the throws lines and the exception outcomes of a boundary contract (`lib/src/failures.rs` for the outcomes, `Graph::throws` in `lib/src/reach.rs` for the exceptions). The exceptions come from the same call graph as the reach lines: a `throw` of a `new`, of a typed local, of what a method returned or a cast produced, the supplier of an `Optional.orElseThrow` (the lambda's return type, or `NoSuchElementException` with no supplier), and Spring's `Assert` (`IllegalStateException` for `state`, `IllegalArgumentException` for the rest). A `catch` on the path that never rethrows its variable swallows what it catches (`HoldService.hold` turns `HoldPolicy`'s `IllegalArgumentException` into `InvalidRequestException` this way); one that does rethrow it, like the retry loop in `Transactions.run` or a `finally`, passes everything through; one that wraps throws the wrapper. What each exception becomes follows Spring's resolution order: an `@ExceptionHandler` in the controller (or a superclass of it) first, then the `@ControllerAdvice` beans in `@Order` (ties by class name), each matched by its `basePackages`, `assignableTypes` and `annotations` when it names any, the closest type up the exception's superclass chain winning within one bean; then a `@ResponseStatus` on the exception's class or a superclass; then the status a `ResponseStatusException` was built with, when it is an `HttpStatus` constant. Two `@ExceptionHandler` methods for one type in one advice are a `!` line: Spring refuses the ambiguity when it builds the advice's resolver at startup.
