examples.title: A Retry-After rewritten around two unchanged refill helpers, proved equal in a second
examples.summary: The wait a refused request is told to make is rewritten from `credited + period - now` to `period - (now - credited)`, around the two refill helpers it calls and leaves alone. Each helper holds a 64-bit division, and relating two copies of each across the versions is more than the solver settles in a minute. The proof takes the unchanged helpers as one function in both versions, never sees their arithmetic, and is done in a second.
notes: On the machine the examples are measured on (JBMC 6.11.0, CaDiCaL), the proof with the helpers shared took 1.3 s over all 2^320 inputs. With `--no-shared-callees`, the search over inputs in [0:20] passed in a second and the search over [-100000:100000] had not finished after 60 s: two 64-bit divisions and two remainders, one of each per version, compared across the versions.

The helpers are shared because both versions call them, their bytecode is identical in both (constant pool references resolved, so a renumbered pool does not count), and they are pure functions of primitives. A helper that reads a field, takes an array, or calls into the JDK beyond its arithmetic is proved as written, as before.

The stub throws what the helper can throw, here `ArithmeticException` from the division, chosen arbitrarily per new arguments: a version that catches it where the other does not is still found to differ (the library's tests cover that case).

A counterexample found on the stub is replayed through the real bytecode first. One that does not reproduce means the rewrite depends on the helpers' arithmetic; the tool says so in a `note:` line and proves the method again with the helpers as written, which for a 64-bit division may still be the time-out this example avoids.

examples.title: A tie-break reordered to group its parameters by kind, proved equal under the stated reordering
examples.summary: The last-writer-wins tie-break took its two writes interleaved, `(tsA, nodeA, tsB, nodeB)`; a developer groups the parameters by kind, timestamps first, and writes the body as the comparison chain the javadoc describes. A regression proof needs the same signature in both versions, and this one changed. The developer states the relation instead, `winner(tsA, nodeA, tsB, nodeB)` from the new parameters, and the proof is of the new method against the previous one called that way, on every input.
notes: The library's test of the same shape (a `(long, int, long, int)` tie-break regrouped as `(long, long, int, int)` and written as a comparison chain) proves in about a second with JBMC and in 0.1 s with the tool's own checker; the measurement on this kernel is the pipeline's.

Without `previousArguments`, the tool refuses: `the previous version takes (long, int, long, int) and the new one (long, long, int, int); give the previous version's arguments as expressions over the new parameters with --before-arguments`. A method renamed or moved is named with `previousSymbol` (`--before-target`) as well.
An input for which an argument expression throws, a division by zero say, is outside the relation and skipped, as an input in the declared scope is; the expressions here cannot throw.

A rewrite that returned the first write only on a strictly positive order is found by the same proof: the library's test shows the counterexample as `winner(tsA=0, tsB=0, nodeA=0, nodeB=0), previously winner(tsA=0, nodeA=0, tsB=0, nodeB=0)`, before 0 and after 1.

examples.title: A cache expiry in milliseconds left expires entries in their last millisecond, found by the relation
examples.summary: The same rewrite as example 123, the expire-after-write boolean turned into the time an entry has left, but in milliseconds, as the cache's metrics report it; callers test `<= 0`. The developer states the relation to the previous version, `previous == (result <= 0)`, and the proof finds an entry with a fraction of a millisecond to go: not expired before, no millisecond left now, so expired. The integer division rounds the last fraction of a millisecond down to none.
notes: The library's test of the same shape finds `remainingMillis(writtenAtNanos=0, ttlNanos=1, nowNanos=0)` with JBMC in about a second, before `false` and after `0`, under the line `the results are not related by previous == (result <= 0)`; the measurement on this kernel is the pipeline's.

The tool's own checker (`--engine native`) finds the same difference in 0.1 s, but on a large input: it has no staged search of small values, and the shrinker's 4000 interpreter runs do not bring three 64-bit values down, so the witness it reports is the raw one. The example runs JBMC.

The scope excludes the inputs outside the module's precondition (a clock reading from before the write, a non-positive time to live, a write before the clock's zero), as in example 123; the counterexample is well inside it, and is found at the first stage of the search, which tries values up to 20.

examples.title: A cache expiry turned from a boolean into the time left, proved expired exactly when none is left
examples.summary: A cache's expire-after-write test returned whether an entry had expired. A developer turns it into the time the entry has left, so that an eviction can be scheduled for the moment it expires and the metrics endpoint can report it, and callers test `<= 0`. A regression proof compares results of one type, and these are a boolean and a long. The developer states how they are related instead, `previous == (result <= 0)`, and the proof is of that relation between the new method and the previous one on every input the cache can pass.
notes: The library's test of the same shape (the same `isExpired` turned into `remainingNanos`) proves in 0.4 s with JBMC and in 0.1 s with the tool's own checker; the measurement on this kernel is the pipeline's.

Without `resultsAgreeWhen`, the tool refuses: `the previous version returns boolean and the new one long; say how the results are related with --results-agree-when, a boolean expression over the new parameters, previous and result`. The relation may also be given when the types are the same and the meaning changed, `result == previous * 1000L` for seconds that became milliseconds.

The scope is the negation of the precondition in `properties.contract` (`writtenAtNanos >= 0 && nowNanos >= writtenAtNanos && ttlNanos > 0`), so that the proof line reads `where !(!(...))`: the relation holds wherever the module's own property is claimed. Without the scope the proof finds inputs outside it on which `ttlNanos - (nowNanos - writtenAtNanos)` overflows, a clock reading from before the write against a time to live near `Long.MAX_VALUE`, which the old comparison of differences survives; those are the inputs the precondition excludes, not a defect of the rewrite.

The relation is checked again on a replayed counterexample, in the interpreter, so that a counterexample from a method JBMC had no bytecode for is recognised as one that does not reproduce, as for an equality.

examples.title: A partitioner rewritten with floorMod keeps every hash on a partition and moves every negative key
examples.summary: Kafka's `toPositive(hash) % n`, with its bit mask, is rewritten as `Math.floorMod(hash, n)`, which also lands every hash on a partition: the module's property still holds and the tests pass. The regression proof, run by the tool's own checker, finds that every negative hash now goes to a different partition than before. Half the keys of a topic move on deploy, and the records of such a key straddle two partitions.
notes: Checked by the tool's own bounded model checker (`approach.engine: native`, the tool's `--engine native`), not JBMC: the method is over two `int` parameters, with a remainder and `Math.floorMod`, both circuits the checker has. The library's run of this shape took 0.4 s: three paths, fifteen solver calls, the witness found in the second stage of the search as `partitionFor(hash=-85120, numPartitions=100000)` and shrunk to `(-1, 3)` in 87 interpreter runs. The measurement on this kernel is the pipeline's.

The checker's search is staged as JBMC's is (inputs in [0:20], then [-100000:100000], then everything), and the stage is reported: `searching inputs in [-100000:100000]` says that the first stage had no counterexample, so every non-negative hash keeps its partition. A path that fails only on large values does not end the search: the checker goes on through the remaining paths, for as long again as the first violation took, in case one of them fails in a smaller stage. Until this cycle the checker returned the first model the solver gave, which for three 64-bit values the shrinker did not bring down (example 122's second note).

The module's property, `result >= 0 && result < numPartitions` for every `numPartitions > 0` (example 023), holds of `floorMod` as it does of the mask, so a property proof passes this change: the property says what every partitioner must do, not that this one does what it did. Regression verification is the check for a cleanup that is meant to change nothing. (The tool's own checker proves that property too, in 53 s: an unsatisfiability proof over a 32-bit remainder is where JBMC's single formula beats path-by-path exploration.)

The disagreement is wide: `hash & 0x7fffffff` is `hash + 2^31` for a negative hash, so the two remainders agree on negative hashes only when the partition count divides 2^31, that is for a count that is a power of two. With 12 partitions, as the tests use, 2^31 leaves a remainder of 8, and every negative hash moves eight partitions along.

examples.title: A JWT skew moved from the window's ends to the clock, proved equal by the tool's own checker
examples.summary: The clock-skew tolerance of a JWT validator is moved from the token's window, `now >= nbf - skew && now < exp + skew`, to the clock, `now + skew >= nbf && now - skew < exp`. Within the module's precondition the two are the same arithmetic, and the tool's own checker proves it in a fraction of a second, with no JBMC; outside it they differ where a sum of seconds overflows a `long`, which the checker also shows when run without the scope.
notes: Checked by the tool's own bounded model checker (`approach.engine: native`, the tool's `--engine native`), which has everything the method needs: four `long` parameters, additions, comparisons, one exception. The library's run of this shape took 0.3 s, eleven paths and 38 solver calls; the measurement on this kernel is the pipeline's. The same proof through JBMC runs the three stages of its search over four longs, each a JBMC process.

Without `intendedInputs`, the checker refutes the change in 0.2 s: `valid(nowSeconds=0, notBefore=-4035225266123908894, expiresAt=0, skewSeconds=5188146770730866915)`, false before and true after, which is the overflow of `notBefore - skewSeconds`. The witness is huge because every witness is: the versions agree wherever no sum overflows, so no stage of the search has one, and the report says so by naming none. The shrinker brings the solver's model down to the values shown in 691 interpreter runs, and no further.

The module's precondition for this method (`properties.contract`) bounds every argument so that the properties about the skew are provable; the scope negates it. A precondition is the right scope for a regression proof, because the proof is then exactly the module's promise: outside what it promises, the versions may differ.

examples.title: A backoff's doubling loop replaced by a shift overflows, found on the record's components
examples.summary: The exponential backoff is a record, `Backoff(baseMillis, capMillis)`, and the delay before an attempt is its method: the base doubled by a loop that stops at the cap. The loop is replaced by `Math.min(capMillis, baseMillis << attempt)`, and the tests pass. The regression proof, which now takes a method of a record and builds the receiver from symbolic components, finds the shift leaving the range of a `long`: a wait of `Long.MIN_VALUE` milliseconds, which a scheduler runs at once, so a failing dependency is retried without pause.
notes: The library's run of this shape took 1.9 s with JBMC, the witness found in the stage `[-100000:100000]` as `delayMillis(this=Backoff[baseMillis=62513, capMillis=65792], attempt=-65528)` and shrunk in 120 interpreter runs; with the scope on the attempt count, 1.9 s and 164 runs. The measurement on this kernel is the pipeline's. The unwinding bound is 32 (`approach.unwind`, the tool's `--unwind`): the loop doubles from a base of at least one up to a cap of at most a day, 2^26.4 milliseconds, so at most 27 turns, and the default of 16 would leave an unwinding assertion unproved.

The receiver is written as `this=Backoff[baseMillis=1, capMillis=1]`, as Java prints a record, and the domain as `this: Backoff(baseMillis: long, capMillis: long) × attempt: int`. In a scope or relation the components are `baseMillis` or `this.baseMillis`, and a record parameter's are `other.component`. An input that a constructor of either version rejects is skipped, as an input outside the scope is: a base of zero or a cap beyond a day is no `Backoff`, so the proof is over the record's invariant, which is where the loop cannot overflow and the shift can. A method identical in both versions is still proved when the record's constructor changed, since the harness builds the receiver through it.

`Math.min` is called by both versions, and the proof first takes it as one function in both (example 120); that counterexample does not reproduce once `min` is computed as written, since the two versions call it on different arguments and an uninterpreted function may answer each as it likes, so the tool says so in a `note:` line and proves again with the callee's bytecode. The second run is the one reported.
The tool's own checker (`--engine native`) does not take this harness: it builds objects, which the checker's integer fragment has no circuits for, and `--engine auto` hands it to JBMC with a note.

examples.title: A backoff's doubling loop replaced by a shift kept short of overflow, proved equal on the record
examples.summary: The same rewrite as example 126, done right: the delay is `baseMillis << attempt` with the shift distance kept below the leading zeros of the base, so that a shift that would leave the range of a `long` is replaced by one that is already past the cap, and a non-positive attempt returns the base. The regression proof on the record's components shows the closed form equal to the loop for every base, cap and attempt the constructor admits, in six seconds.
notes: The library's run of this shape took 6.2 s with JBMC: three stages, three properties (the assertion and the two unwinding assertions), the loop unwound 32 times. The measurement on this kernel is the pipeline's.

As in example 126, `Math.min` is first taken as one function in both versions, which here gives a counterexample that does not reproduce (the two versions call `min` on different arguments), so the proof is run again with the callee's bytecode; the time above includes both runs.

The constructor's bounds are what make the loop and the closed form equal: without the cap's bound of a day, a cap above 2^62 would let the loop's `delay * 2` overflow where the guarded shift does not, and the proof would find it. The harness skips an input the constructor rejects, so the proof is over the record's invariant and nothing weaker; a change that loosened the constructor would widen the statement, and the harness builds the receiver through the constructor of each version.
